beats.intro: Chapter eight, lesson seven. Temperature, pH, cofactors and inhibitors. [[line]]A factory line runs best when its thermostat is set right, and when nobody drops a wrench into the gears. [[cells]]Enzymes are the same. [[strip]]Here is our pathway again, with enzyme one lit. [[local]]Today we ask what its surroundings, and some chemical visitors, do to it.
beats.temp: [[cond]]An enzyme's activity depends on general conditions, such as temperature and pH, and on chemicals that act on it specifically. [[opt]]Every enzyme has an optimal temperature, where its shape is the most active. [[human]]For a typical human enzyme, that is about thirty seven degrees Celsius. [[hot]]An enzyme from heat tolerant bacteria, living in hot springs, peaks near seventy seven degrees Celsius. [[cold]]Cooler than the optimum, the molecules move slowly, so the rate falls. [[denat]]Hotter, and the shape unravels. The enzyme is denatured, and the rate crashes to almost nothing. [[note]]Notice that the human enzyme has stopped by about fifty degrees, while the bacterial one is still running. [[fever]]That is one reason a very high fever is dangerous: some of the body's enzymes begin to lose their shape.
beats.ph: [[ph]]The pH works the same way. Each enzyme has an optimal pH. [[pepsin]]Pepsin, a stomach enzyme, works best around pH two, which is very acidic. [[trypsin]]Trypsin, an intestinal enzyme, works best around pH eight, which is slightly basic. [[swap]]Drop pepsin into the intestine, and it loses its shape, and its job. [[shape]]In every case, optimal conditions favor the most active shape for the enzyme.
beats.q1: Quick check. Why does a human enzyme almost stop at sixty degrees Celsius?
beats.cofactor: [[cof]]Some enzymes need a helper. Cofactors are nonprotein enzyme helpers. [[metal]]Some are inorganic, such as a metal ion like zinc or iron. [[coen]]An organic cofactor is called a coenzyme, and many coenzymes are made from vitamins. [[need]]Without its helper, the enzyme cannot do its job. [[diet]]Many enzymes hold a zinc or an iron ion right in the active site, where it helps grip the substrate. That is one reason we need small amounts of these minerals, and of vitamins, in our diet.
beats.compet: [[inhib]]Other chemicals are inhibitors, and they come in two kinds. [[comp]]A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate. It binds to the active site, and competes with the substrate for entry, like a look-alike key jammed in a lock. [[block]]While it sits there, the substrate is shut out. [[more]]But it is a numbers game. Add more substrate, and the substrate wins the active sites more often. So this kind of inhibition can be overcome by increasing the concentration of substrate.
beats.noncomp: [[non]]A noncompetitive inhibitor binds to another part of the enzyme, not the active site. [[shape]]That makes the enzyme change shape, and the active site becomes less effective. [[nomore]]The substrate fits badly, however much of it there is, so extra substrate does not fully fix it. [[sarin]]Toxins and poisons are often irreversible inhibitors. Sarin, a nerve gas, binds covalently to a serine in the active site of acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme of the nervous system, and it stays bound. [[irr]]Sarin is not a noncompetitive inhibitor: it binds the active site itself, permanently. It is an irreversible poison. With that enzyme jammed, nerve signals cannot be switched off.
beats.q2: Quick check. Sort each clue: does it describe a competitive inhibitor, or a noncompetitive one?
beats.example: Let's try a worked case. [[a]]An enzyme and its substrate run at a steady rate. [[b]]Add a competitive inhibitor, and the rate drops. [[c]]Now flood in more substrate. The rate climbs back toward where it was. [[d]]Do the same with a noncompetitive inhibitor, and the rate stays well below, however much substrate you add. [[e]]So a simple test tells the two apart. Add more substrate. If the rate recovers, the inhibitor is competitive. If it does not, it is noncompetitive.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[sum1]]Temperature and pH set the enzyme's shape. Too far from the optimum, and it is denatured. [[sum2]]Cofactors and coenzymes help it work. [[sum3]]Competitive inhibitors block the active site, and more substrate beats them. Noncompetitive inhibitors change the shape, and more substrate does not. [[end]]Now try the practice.
